slides.text: By day four of sequestered deliberations in the Blackwood murder trial, eleven of us were ready to convict the defendant. Only Juror Eight—a soft-spoken retired postal worker named Arthur—held out for not guilty. 'Look at the crime scene photo of the study,' Arthur said quietly, tapping the glossy print. 'The killer was left-handed. Look at the angle of the broken brass candlestick.'

I frowned, leaning over the mahogany table. I’m the jury foreperson, and I had taken forty pages of notes during the trial. 'Arthur, the prosecution never mentioned a brass candlestick. It wasn't in the evidence log, and it’s cropped out of this photograph.' The room went dead silent. Eleven pairs of eyes turned slowly toward the end of the table.

Arthur didn't flinch. With his left hand, he calmly closed his manila folder and smiled. 'If we convict the boy on the stand, his appellate lawyers will eventually reopen the investigation,' he said softly. 'If we acquit him today, double jeopardy attaches, the file goes into the basement forever, and nobody ever looks for the candlestick.' Then he looked at the locked door. 'Now, shall we take another vote?'
